title: The Blaschka Object Network — Ware Collection Transatlantic Logistics and Customs Register
scope: Repeated transatlantic shipment infrastructure for the Blaschka botanical models, with emphasis on named forwarding agents, ocean carriers, customs brokers, customs inspection, insurance, freight charges, packing materials and receiving-side clearance. The purpose is to reconstruct transport as a chain of institutions and documents rather than a single 'shipped to Harvard' event.
methodological_guard: Adjacent letters and invoices are cross-walked only when date, case marks, consignee, carrier or archival sequence supports the connection. Corporate archives are listed as retrieval targets; their existence does not prove survival of a particular Blaschka cargo record. Shipping agents, ocean carriers, customs brokers, customs authorities and Harvard officers remain separate roles.

source_base.customs_archives: U.S. National Archives Record Group 36, Records of the U.S. Customs Service

routes.research_value: The 1929 chain shows packing material itself becoming a regulated object. The same material that protected fragile glass during transport could trigger customs or plant-quarantine intervention at the border.

external_archive_targets.survival_guard: The finding aid explicitly warns that the Bremen holdings are only a small remnant of the former company archive. Around 1,000 ship files with photographs, voyage reports, passenger lists and cargo papers were transferred to the Hapag-Lloyd archive in Hamburg. The corresponding Hamburg ship-file list shown in the Bremen finding aid mainly documents later vessels/dates, so no early Blaschka cargo file is assumed to survive.

external_archive_targets.reference: Record Group 36, Records of the U.S. Customs Service
external_archive_targets.coverage: Boston customs records extend across the Blaschka shipment period; the national guide lists Boston-Charlestown records 1789–1918 and Boston regional holdings 1858–1966, while the Boston holdings page lists customs field records into the twentieth century.
external_archive_targets.research_question: Can the 1906, 1923 or 1929 Harvard Blaschka consignments be matched to Boston customs entry, bonded-movement, manifest, warehouse or inspection records?

external_archive_targets.evidence_of_business: The firm recurs in Blaschka records from Rudolf's 1892 travel arrangements through multiple Harvard shipments in 1906, 1923 and 1929.
external_archive_targets.next_search: Bremen commercial registers, address books, chamber-of-commerce records and forwarding-agent archives; no dedicated fonds has yet been confidently identified.

external_archive_targets.evidence_of_business: Harvard correspondence identifies E. A. Snow as a State Street custom-house broker and forwarding agent and shows repeated use of his name as consignee even after his business status changed.
external_archive_targets.next_search: Boston city/business directories and customs-broker licensing/administrative records before asserting a firm identity or successor.

external_archive_targets.evidence_of_business: The Blaschka archive itself preserves a 20 October 1923 T. D. Downing Co. customs/freight invoice to Harvard, giving a direct company document even without a separate corporate archive.
external_archive_targets.next_search: Boston/New York commercial directories, customs-broker licensing records and receiving-side Harvard Treasurer records.

research_observation: Across 1906, 1923 and 1929 the Harvard route repeatedly reuses the same categories of intermediary while particular firms and regulations change. Forwarders, carriers, brokers, customs officers, bonded movement, consular invoices, insurance, packing materials, clearance and local repair formed a durable logistics apparatus around the glass models. This creates a longitudinal source base for studying how fragility was administratively managed rather than treating transport as an isolated accident between workshop and museum.
